events.label: The pair of giants is separated from the pair of red dwarfs by 723”.
A major milestone in stellar X-ray astronomy happened on April 5, 1974.
In 1975, an eccentric 388-year orbit gave masses of 0.65 M☉ and 0.13 M☉.
In 2015 the separation had increased to 3.5″.

medium.text: Capella is the sixth-brightest star in the night sky, and the third-brightest in the northern celestial hemisphere after Arcturus and Vega.
Several other stars in the same visual field have been catalogued as companions but are physically unrelated.

events.label: The pair of giants is separated from the pair of red dwarfs by 723”.
A major milestone in stellar X-ray astronomy happened on April 5, 1974.
In 1975, an eccentric 388-year orbit gave masses of 0.65 M☉ and 0.13 M☉.
In 2015 the separation had increased to 3.5″.

deep.text: As a relatively nearby star system, Capella is listed in the Gliese-Jahreiss Catalogue with designations GJ 194 for the bright pair of giants and GJ 195 for the faint pair of red dwarfs.
Capella was the brightest star in the night sky from 210,000 years ago to 160,000 years ago, at about −1.8 in apparent magnitude.
At −1.1, Aldebaran was brightest before this period; it and Capella were situated rather close to each other in the sky and approximated boreal pole stars at the time.

With an average apparent magnitude of +0.08, Capella is the brightest object in the constellation Auriga, the sixth-brightest star in the night sky, the third-brightest in the northern celestial hemisphere.
α Aurigae is the star system’s Bayer designation.

Based on an annual parallax shift of 76.20 milliarcseconds as measured by the Hipparcos satellite, this system is estimated to be 42.8 light-years from Earth, with a margin of error of 0.3 light-year.
Several other stars in the same visual field have been catalogued as companions but are physically unrelated.
